turns.prompt_text: I would like to be able to upload files received from my gmail onto a databas
turns.response_html:
This is a classic data pipeline challenge. Since you have a background in software engineering, I will skip the generic advice and focus on the architectural decisions and technical implementation methods suited to a developer.

There are three primary ways to architect this, depending on whether you want to write code or use an automation tool.

Phase 1: Architectural Decision (BLOB vs. Reference)

Before writing a script, you must decide how the file resides in the database.

  1. The "Reference" Method (Recommended):

    • Workflow: You upload the actual file to an Object Store (Google Drive, AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage). You then generate a URL/Path for that file and insert that string into your database.
    • Pros: Keeps your database lean; faster backups; databases are generally poor at serving large binaries.
    • Cons: You have to manage permissions for two systems (DB and Storage).

  2. The "BLOB" Method:

    • Workflow: You convert the file into binary data (Binary Large Object) and insert it directly into a column in your database.
    • Pros: Transactional integrity (the file and metadata succeed or fail together).
    • Cons: Bloats the database quickly; performance degradation on queries.

Phase 2: Implementation Options

Option A: The "Native" Way (Google Apps Script)

This is often the fastest route because it runs directly within Google’s infrastructure, requiring no server setup or complex authentication handshakes.

  • Best for: Small-to-medium volume, personal projects, sending data to Google Sheets, BigQuery, or JDBC-supported SQL databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle).
  • How it works:
    1. Open Google Drive -> New -> More -> Google Apps Script.
    2. Use the GmailApp class to fetch threads/messages.
    3. Use Jdbc service to connect to your external database.

Pseudo-code Example:

function saveAttachmentsToDB() {
  // 1. Get unread messages with attachments
  var threads = GmailApp.search('has:attachment is:unread label:Work');
  
  // 2. Connect to DB
  var conn = Jdbc.getConnection("jdbc:mysql://<IP>:3306/<DB_NAME>", "user", "password");
  var stmt = conn.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO files (filename, file_data) VALUES (?, ?)");

  for (var i = 0; i < threads.length; i++) {
    var messages = threads[i].getMessages();
    for (var j = 0; j < messages.length; j++) {
      var attachments = messages[j].getAttachments();
      for (var k = 0; k < attachments.length; k++) {
        
        // 3. Convert to Blob and Insert
        var fileBlob = attachments[k];
        stmt.setString(1, fileBlob.getName());
        stmt.setBlob(2, fileBlob); // Direct BLOB insertion
        stmt.addBatch();
      }
    }
  }
  stmt.executeBatch();
  conn.close();
}

Option B: The "Engineer" Way (Python)

If you are processing the files (e.g., parsing a CSV before upload, resizing images) or using a database not supported by Google Apps Script (like MongoDB or a local SQLite), use Python.

  • Best for: Complex data transformation, heavy automation, local databases.
  • Tools: google-api-python-client (for Gmail), SQLAlchemy (for DB).
  • Authentication: You will need to set up a Service Account or OAuth 2.0 credentials in the Google Cloud Console to allow your script to access your Gmail.

Workflow:

  1. Authenticate: Use google.oauth2.credentials to authorize the Gmail API.
  2. Fetch: service.users().messages().list() to find emails.
  3. Download: service.users().messages().attachments().get() to pull the bytes.
  4. Upload: Use psycopg2 (Postgres) or pymysql to insert.

Option C: The "No-Code" Way (Zapier / Make)

If you don't want to maintain a script, use an iPaaS (Integration Platform as a Service).

  • Best for: Quick setup, low maintenance, non-sensitive data.
  • Tool: Make (formerly Integromat) is generally better than Zapier for this because it handles binary file data better.
  • Workflow:
    • Module 1 (Trigger): Watch Gmail (Filter: Has Attachment).
    • Module 2 (Iterator): Iterate through attachments (if multiple).
    • Module 3 (Action): PostgreSQL/MySQL "Execute Query" -> Insert the binary data or upload to S3 and insert the link.

Which database are you targeting?

turns.prompt_text: Can we target a Google Sheets as a database? Or are there better options?
turns.response_html:
Yes, you can target Google Sheets, but if you have a software engineering background, you will likely find it frustrating if you try to treat it like a traditional database (SQL/NoSQL).

Here is the breakdown of why, how to do it correctly, and what the superior options are.

The Verdict on Google Sheets

Can it be a database? Yes, for metadata. Can it store files (BLOBs)? No.

While you technically can Base64 encode a file and shove it into a cell, Google Sheets has a limit of 50,000 characters per cell. A typical PDF or image will exceed this instantly. Furthermore, loading a sheet full of Base64 strings will crash your browser.

The "Right" Way to Use Google Sheets (The Reference Pattern)

If you want to use the Google ecosystem, the standard architectural pattern is Google Drive + Google Sheets.

  1. Storage: The script saves the file attachment to a specific Google Drive Folder.
  2. Database: The script takes the Shareable URL (WebLink) of that file and writes it to a row in Google Sheets, along with metadata (Sender, Date, Subject).

Pros:

  • Zero Cost: Uses your existing Drive storage.
  • Visual: You can easily see the log of files and click the link to open them.
  • Zero Ops: No server to spin up; Google Apps Script handles the cron jobs (triggers).

Cons:

  • Not Queryable: You can't run SQL queries like SELECT * WHERE.
  • Fragile: If you move the file in Drive manually, the link in Sheets might break (unless you store the immutable ID).

Better Options (Ranked by Complexity)

If you need more than just a log of links, consider these alternatives:

1. Airtable (The "Better Sheets")

If you want the visual simplicity of a spreadsheet but the power of a database, Airtable is superior to Sheets for this specific task.

  • Why: It has a native "Attachment" field type.
  • How it works: You send the file to Airtable's API, and it actually hosts the file within the "cell" (visualized as a thumbnail). You don't need a separate cloud storage bucket.
  • Best For: When you want to browse files visually without writing code to manage storage links.

2. Firebase (Firestore + Cloud Storage)

Since you are a developer, this is likely the most satisfying "Serverless" approach.

  • Why: It keeps you in the Google Cloud ecosystem but uses "real" tools.
  • How it works:
    • Google Cloud Storage: Holds the actual files.
    • Firestore (NoSQL): Stores the metadata (JSON) and the gs:// path to the file.
  • Best For: If you plan to build a frontend app later that needs to fetch and display these files.

3. PostgreSQL + S3 (The Industry Standard)

If this is for a production system or a resume project.

  • Why: Relational integrity and cheap storage.
  • How it works: Python script pulls email -> uploads to AWS S3 -> inserts record into RDS/PostgreSQL.
  • Best For: High volume, complex querying, or if you need to perform analytics on the metadata.

The Solution: Google Drive + Sheets (Code Snippet)

Since you are likely looking for the quickest "set and forget" solution, here is the Google Apps Script to implement the Drive + Sheets pattern.

  1. Create a Google Sheet.
  2. Go to Extensions > Apps Script.
  3. Paste this code:
function saveGmailAttachmentsToDriveAndSheet() {
  // CONFIGURATION
  var folderId = 'YOUR_GOOGLE_DRIVE_FOLDER_ID'; // The ID part of the Drive URL
  var sheetName = 'Sheet1';
  var labelName = 'To_Process'; // Create this label in Gmail to filter what gets saved
  
  var folder = DriveApp.getFolderById(folderId);
  var sheet = SpreadsheetApp.getActiveSpreadsheet().getSheetByName(sheetName);
  
  // Find threads with the label
  var threads = GmailApp.getUserLabelByName(labelName).getThreads();
  
  for (var i = 0; i < threads.length; i++) {
    var messages = threads[i].getMessages();
    
    for (var j = 0; j < messages.length; j++) {
      var msg = messages[j];
      var attachments = msg.getAttachments();
      
      for (var k = 0; k < attachments.length; k++) {
        var attachment = attachments[k];
        
        // 1. Save to Drive
        var file = folder.createFile(attachment);
        
        // 2. Write Metadata to Sheet
        // Columns: [Date, Sender, Subject, Filename, Drive_URL]
        sheet.appendRow([
          msg.getDate(),
          msg.getFrom(),
          msg.getSubject(),
          file.getName(),
          file.getUrl()
        ]);
      }
    }
    
    // Optional: Remove label so it doesn't process again
    threads[i].removeLabel(GmailApp.getUserLabelByName(labelName));
  }
}

turns.response_html:
Here is the step-by-step implementation plan to automate converting Excel attachments from Gmail into native Google Sheets in your Drive.

Since you are a developer, I have stripped out the fluff and focused on the configuration and API hooks.

Phase 1: Environment Setup

  1. Create a Target Folder (Google Drive):

    • Create a new folder in Drive where these files will live.
    • Action: Open the folder and look at the URL. Copy the alphanumeric string at the end (e.g., 1aBcDeFgHiJkLmNoP...). This is your Folder ID.

  2. Create a Trigger Label (Gmail):

    • Create a specific label in Gmail (e.g., To_Convert) and apply it to an email that has an Excel attachment for testing.
    • Tip: You can set up a Gmail Filter later to automatically apply this label to incoming emails from specific senders.

Phase 2: The Script Configuration

  1. Open the Editor:

    • Go to script.google.com.
    • Click "New Project".

  2. Enable the Advanced Drive API (Critical Step):

    • Standard DriveApp cannot convert files; you need the advanced REST API wrapper.
    • On the left sidebar, click the + (Plus) next to Services.
    • Scroll down, select Drive API, and click Add.
    • Verify: You should see "Drive" appear under the Services list.

  3. Deploy the Code:

    • Delete the default myFunction and paste this engineer-ready code. I have added error handling and logging suitable for debugging.
function processExcelAttachments() {
  // --- USER CONFIGURATION ---
  const FOLDER_ID = 'PASTE_YOUR_FOLDER_ID_HERE'; 
  const GMAIL_LABEL = 'To_Convert';
  // --------------------------

  // MimeTypes to target (XLS and XLSX)
  const MS_EXCEL_TYPES = [
    "application/vnd.ms-excel",
    "application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet"
  ];

  const label = GmailApp.getUserLabelByName(GMAIL_LABEL);
  
  // Guard clause: If label doesn't exist or has no threads, exit
  if (!label) { Logger.log("Label not found."); return; }
  const threads = label.getThreads();
  if (threads.length === 0) { Logger.log("No threads to process."); return; }

  // Iterate threads
  threads.forEach(thread => {
    const messages = thread.getMessages();
    
    messages.forEach(msg => {
      const attachments = msg.getAttachments();
      
      attachments.forEach(attachment => {
        const type = attachment.getContentType();
        
        // Check if it's an Excel file
        if (MS_EXCEL_TYPES.includes(type)) {
          try {
            // Define the metadata for the API request
            const resource = {
              name: attachment.getName().replace(/\.xlsx?$/, ""), // Strip extension
              parents: [FOLDER_ID],
              mimeType: MimeType.GOOGLE_SHEETS // This triggers the conversion
            };

            // Call Advanced Drive API
            const file = Drive.Files.create(resource, attachment.copyBlob());
            Logger.log(`SUCCESS: Converted '${file.name}' (ID: ${file.id})`);
            
          } catch (e) {
            Logger.log(`ERROR: Failed to convert '${attachment.getName()}'. Reason: ${e.message}`);
          }
        }
      });
    });

    // Cleanup: Remove label so it doesn't process endlessly
    thread.removeLabel(label);
  });
}

Phase 3: Automation (The "Cron Job")

You don't want to run this manually every time.

  1. In the Apps Script sidebar, click the Alarm Clock icon (Triggers).
  2. Click + Add Trigger (bottom right).
  3. Configure as follows:
    • Function to run: processExcelAttachments
    • Event Source: Time-driven
    • Type of time based trigger: Hour timer
    • Interval: Every hour (or Every minute if you need near real-time).
  4. Click Save. Google will ask for permissions one last time to access your Gmail and Drive.

How to Test It

  1. Send yourself an email with an Excel attachment.
  2. Apply the To_Convert label to that email.
  3. Go back to the script editor and click Run (the Play button) manually for the first test.
  4. Check the Execution Log (at the bottom) for "SUCCESS".
  5. Check your Google Drive folder—you should see the green Google Sheet file there.

Next Step

Once this is running, you will have a folder filling up with individual Google Sheets.

Would you like the logic to merge these new sheets into a single Master Database Sheet automatically, or do you prefer keeping them as separate files?

Since you are looking to build a true data pipeline (ETL), we will modify the previous script to include the Transformation and Loading steps.

We will update the script to perform these actions in a single pass:

  1. Extract: Grab the Excel file from Gmail.
  2. Transform: Convert it to a temporary Google Sheet and strip the header row (so your master database doesn't have repeated headers).
  3. Load: Append the data to your "Master Database" Sheet.
  4. Cleanup: Optionally delete the temporary file to keep your Drive clean.

Prerequisites

  1. Create your "Master Database" Sheet: Create a new Google Sheet. Set up the header row (Row 1) exactly how you want it.
  2. Get the ID: Copy the ID from the URL of this Master Sheet.

The Full ETL Script

Replace the previous code with this version. I have added a mergeData helper function to handle the array manipulation.

function processAndMergeExcelAttachments() {
  // --- CONFIGURATION ---
  const FOLDER_ID = 'YOUR_DRIVE_FOLDER_ID';     // Where files are saved/converted
  const MASTER_SHEET_ID = 'YOUR_MASTER_SHEET_ID'; // The database sheet
  const GMAIL_LABEL = 'To_Convert';
  const KEEP_ARCHIVE = true; // Set to false to delete the converted file after merging
  // ---------------------

  const MS_EXCEL_TYPES = [
    "application/vnd.ms-excel",
    "application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet"
  ];

  const label = GmailApp.getUserLabelByName(GMAIL_LABEL);
  if (!label) { Logger.log("Label not found."); return; }
  
  const threads = label.getThreads();
  if (threads.length === 0) { Logger.log("No threads to process."); return; }

  // Open Master Sheet once to save I/O time
  const masterSS = SpreadsheetApp.openById(MASTER_SHEET_ID);
  const masterSheet = masterSS.getSheets()[0]; // Assuming data goes to the first tab

  threads.forEach(thread => {
    const messages = thread.getMessages();
    
    messages.forEach(msg => {
      const attachments = msg.getAttachments();
      
      attachments.forEach(attachment => {
        if (MS_EXCEL_TYPES.includes(attachment.getContentType())) {
          try {
            // 1. CONVERT (Drive API)
            const resource = {
              name: attachment.getName().replace(/\.xlsx?$/, ""),
              parents: [FOLDER_ID],
              mimeType: MimeType.GOOGLE_SHEETS
            };
            
            // This creates the file in Drive
            const convertedFile = Drive.Files.create(resource, attachment.copyBlob());
            Logger.log(`Converted: ${convertedFile.name}`);

            // 2. EXTRACT DATA
            const tempSS = SpreadsheetApp.openById(convertedFile.id);
            const tempSheet = tempSS.getSheets()[0];
            const dataRange = tempSheet.getDataRange();
            const data = dataRange.getValues();

            // 3. TRANSFORM & LOAD
            // Check if there is data beyond the header
            if (data.length > 1) {
              // Remove the first row (Header) so we don't duplicate it
              // Comment this line out if your source files DO NOT have headers
              data.shift(); 

              // Append to Master
              // getRange(row, col, numRows, numCols)
              const lastRow = masterSheet.getLastRow();
              masterSheet.getRange(lastRow + 1, 1, data.length, data[0].length).setValues(data);
              
              Logger.log(`Merged ${data.length} rows into Master DB.`);
            }

            // 4. CLEANUP
            if (!KEEP_ARCHIVE) {
              Drive.Files.remove(convertedFile.id);
            }

          } catch (e) {
            Logger.log(`ERROR processing ${attachment.getName()}: ${e.message}`);
          }
        }
      });
    });

    // Remove label from email
    thread.removeLabel(label);
  });
}

Engineer's Notes on Schema Validation

Since you have a background in software engineering, you know that "Schema Drift" is the enemy here. This script assumes a Happy Path:

  1. Column Order: It assumes every Excel file has the exact same columns in the exact same order. If one sender swaps "First Name" and "Last Name", your database will be corrupted.
  2. Data Types: It assumes the data types match.

If you anticipate inconsistent columns: You would need to write a "Mapper" function. Instead of data.shift(), you would:

  1. Read the header row of the incoming file (data[0]).
  2. Compare it to a hardcoded map of your Master Sheet headers.
  3. Re-map the array indices before appending.

function processSheetsWithDateHeaders() {
  var ss = SpreadsheetApp.getActiveSpreadsheet();
  var sheets = ss.getSheets();

  // Iterate through every sheet in the file
  sheets.forEach(function(sheet) {
    var sheetName = sheet.getName();

    var headers = headerRange.getValues()[0];

    // --- DECISION LOGIC ---
    // We check the first non-empty cell in the header.
    // If it is a Date object, we proceed.
    if (isHeaderRowDates(headers)) {
      Logger.log("✅ MATCH: Sheet '" + sheetName + "' has dates in the first row. Gathering data...");
      
      // *** YOUR DATA GATHERING LOGIC GOES HERE ***
      // Example: var data = sheet.getDataRange().getValues();
      
    } else {
      Logger.log("❌ SKIP: Sheet '" + sheetName + "' does not appear to have dates in row 1.");
    }
  });
}

// Helper function to determine if the row contains dates
function isHeaderRowDates(rowValues) {
  // We check the first cell. You can loop through 'rowValues' to check all if preferred.
  var firstCell = rowValues[0];

  // Check 1: Is it strictly a Date object? (Google Sheets default behavior for dates)
  if (Object.prototype.toString.call(firstCell) === '[object Date]') {
    return true;
  }

  // Check 2: Is it a string that looks like a date? (e.g., "2025-01-01")
  // Only use this if your dates might be formatted as Plain Text
  var timestamp = Date.parse(firstCell);
  if (isNaN(timestamp) == false) {
    return true;
  }

  return false;
}

Key Considerations for "Date" Detection

When working with "intuition" in code, we have to define exactly what constitutes a date, as spreadsheets can be messy:

  • Strict Typing: Google Sheets treats dates as Objects. If you type 12/25/2025 into a cell, it becomes an Object. The script prioritizes this.
  • Loose Typing: Sometimes a user types '12/25/2025 (with an apostrophe) to force it to be text. The "Check 2" in the script handles this by attempting to parse the text into a time format.
  • The "First Cell" Rule: These scripts currently check the first cell of the first row. If your sheets have a label in A1 (like "Timeline") and the dates start in B1, you will need to adjust the index from 0 to 1.

import pandas as pd
import datetime
from dateutil.parser import parse

def is_date(item):
    """
    Helper function to determine if a single item is a valid date.
    Returns True if it is a datetime object or a parseable date string.
    """
    if pd.isna(item):
        return False
    
    # Check if it's already a timestamp/datetime object
    if isinstance(item, (pd.Timestamp, datetime.datetime, datetime.date)):
        return True
        
    # If it's a string, try to parse it
    if isinstance(item, str):
        try:
            # fuzzy=False ensures we don't match things like "Item 1" as dates
            parse(item, fuzzy=False)
            return True
        except (ValueError, TypeError):
            return False
            
    return False

def check_header_row_for_dates(df_head):
    """
    Analyzes the first row of the dataframe.
    Returns True if the majority of the non-empty cells in the first row are dates.
    """
    if df_head.empty:
        return False

    # Get the first row (headers)
    first_row = df_head.columns.tolist()
    
    date_count = 0
    total_checked = 0

    for cell in first_row:
        # We allow ignoring 'Unnamed' columns which Pandas creates for empty header cells
        if str(cell).startswith('Unnamed'):
            continue
            
        total_checked += 1
        if is_date(cell):
            date_count += 1

    # Heuristic: If > 50% of the headers are dates, we accept this sheet
    # You can adjust this threshold (e.g., to 1 for "at least one date")
    if total_checked > 0 and (date_count / total_checked) > 0.5:
        return True
    
    return False

              Logger.log(`✅ Success: '${newFileName}' saved. Kept ${validSchedules.length} sheets, deleted ${junkSheets.length} junk sheets.`);

// --- HELPER FUNCTION ---
function isHeaderRowDates(sheet) {
  var lastCol = sheet.getLastColumn();
  if (lastCol === 0) return false; 

  var headerValues = sheet.getRange(1, 1, 1, lastCol).getValues()[0];
  
  var dateCount = 0;
  var totalCells = headerValues.length;
  
  for (var i = 0; i < totalCells; i++) {
    var cell = headerValues[i];
    
    // Check 1: Strict Google Sheets Date Object
    if (Object.prototype.toString.call(cell) === '[object Date]') {
      dateCount++;
      continue;
    }

    // Check 2: String parsing (e.g. "10/12" or "Mon 10/12")
    if (typeof cell === 'string' && (cell.includes('/') || cell.includes('-'))) {
      var timestamp = Date.parse(cell);
      if (!isNaN(timestamp)) {
        dateCount++;
      }
    }
  }

  // Threshold: If > 30% of headers are dates, it's a schedule
  return (dateCount / totalCells) > 0.3;
}

Summary of Logic

  1. Ingest: It takes the Excel file and converts it to a Google Sheet immediately.
  2. Audit: It scans every tab and splits them into two lists: validSchedules and junkSheets.
  3. Kill Switch:
    • If validSchedules is empty (0), it immediately calls Drive.Files.remove on the entire file ID. It never saves.
    • If validSchedules has items, it proceeds to delete the junkSheets and keeps the file.

turns.prompt_text: All right. So I already have a very nice gooey setup through a lovable website. However, I'm having trouble accessing the information. from lovable I think I need to set up a Google service. account
turns.response_html:
This makes perfect sense now. You are building a Headless Architecture:

  1. Backend: Google Sheets (acting as your database).
  2. Middleware: Google Apps Script (automating the data entry from email).
  3. Frontend: Your Lovable website (displaying the data).
  4. The Key: The Google Service Account is the "security badge" that lets your Lovable website talk to your private Google Sheet without asking you to log in every time.

Here is the exact roadmap to connect these dots.

Part 1: The Data Structure (Crucial Adjustment)

You previously asked to just "save the Excel file." We cannot do that anymore. A website cannot easily "read" a closed Excel file inside a Drive folder.

We must go back to the Parsing Script. Your Lovable website needs a Master Google Sheet with clean rows (Date, Name, Shift) to query.

Action:

  1. Create a new Google Sheet. Name it "Fareway_Master_DB".
  2. Create headers in Row 1: Employee Name, Job Type, Date, Start Time, End Time, Total Hours.
  3. Copy the ID of this sheet (found in the URL between /d/ and /edit).

Part 2: The Service Account ( The Bridge)

You were on the right track asking for the keys. Here is how to set it up so Lovable can read that sheet.

Step A: Get the Key

  1. Go to the Google Cloud Console.
  2. Create a Project (e.g., "Fareway-Schedule-App").
  3. Go to IAM & Admin > Service Accounts.
  4. Click Create Service Account. Name it "sheet-reader".
  5. Click Done.
  6. Click on the email address of the new account (e.g., sheet-reader@project-id.iam.gserviceaccount.com).
  7. Go to the Keys tab > Add Key > Create New Key > JSON.
  8. Save this file. This is what you will upload/paste into your Lovable project or backend code.

Step B: Enable the API

  1. In Google Cloud Console, search for "Google Sheets API" in the top bar.
  2. Click Enable.

Step C: Share the Sheet (The Most Common Mistake)

  1. Open your "Fareway_Master_DB" Google Sheet.
  2. Click the big Share button.
  3. Paste the Service Account Email (the one ending in @...iam.gserviceaccount.com).
  4. Give it Editor access.
  5. Uncheck "Notify people" and click Share.

Part 3: The Script (The Engine)

Now we need the script that takes the email and pushes it into that specific Master Sheet so your website has fresh data to pull.

Here is the Parsing Script tailored for this Database approach:

function processScheduleToMasterDB() {
  // --- CONFIGURATION ---
  // 1. Put your Master Sheet ID here (from Part 1)
  const MASTER_SHEET_ID = 'YOUR_GOOGLE_SHEET_ID_HERE'; 
  const GMAIL_LABEL = 'Fareway';
  
  // 2. Mapping Fareway codes to real words
  const SECTION_MAP = {
    'D': 'Dairy', 'DAIRY': 'Dairy',
    'O': 'Office', 'OFFICE': 'Office',
    'PRODUCE': 'Produce', 'CHECKERS': 'Checkers',
    'FULL-TIME': 'Full-Time', 'PART-TIME': 'Part-Time'
  };
  // ---------------------

  const masterSS = SpreadsheetApp.openById(MASTER_SHEET_ID);
  const masterSheet = masterSS.getSheets()[0]; // Assumes data goes on first tab
  const label = GmailApp.getUserLabelByName(GMAIL_LABEL);
  const threads = label.getThreads();

  if (threads.length === 0) return;

  threads.forEach(thread => {
    const msgs = thread.getMessages();
    msgs.forEach(msg => {
      const attachments = msg.getAttachments();
      attachments.forEach(att => {
        // Check for Excel
        if (att.getContentType().includes("excel") || att.getContentType().includes("spreadsheet")) {
          
          // Convert Excel to temporary Sheet to read it
          let resource = { title: att.getName(), mimeType: MimeType.GOOGLE_SHEETS };
          let tempFile = Drive.Files.create(resource, att.copyBlob());
          let tempSS = SpreadsheetApp.openById(tempFile.id);
          let sheets = tempSS.getSheets();

          sheets.forEach(sheet => {
            // Check for dates in header to confirm it's a schedule
            let headers = sheet.getRange(1, 1, 1, sheet.getLastColumn()).getValues()[0];
            if (!isHeaderRowDates(headers)) return;

            let data = sheet.getDataRange().getValues();
            let rowsToPush = [];
            let currentType = "General";

            // Start parsing from Row 3 (Index 2)
            for (let i = 2; i < data.length; i++) {
              let row = data[i];
              let name = row[0].toString().trim();
              
              if (!name || name === 'TOTAL') continue;

              // Check if this row is actually a Section Header (like "DAIRY")
              if (SECTION_MAP[name.toUpperCase()] || name.length < 3) {
                currentType = SECTION_MAP[name.toUpperCase()] || name;
                continue;
              }

              // Extract the week's dates from the header
              // We loop through columns 1-7 (Mon-Sun)
              for (let col = 1; col <= 7; col++) {
                let cellValue = row[col];
                if (cellValue && cellValue.toString().length > 0) {
                  // Determine the specific date for this column
                  // (Logic assumes header contains dates)
                  let dateObj = headers[col]; 
                  
                  // Add row to our database array
                  rowsToPush.push([
                    name,           // Employee Name
                    currentType,    // Job Type
                    dateObj,        // Date
                    cellValue,      // Shift (e.g. "8-4") or Hours
                  ]);
                }
              }
            }

            // Push to Master DB
            if (rowsToPush.length > 0) {
              masterSheet.getRange(masterSheet.getLastRow() + 1, 1, rowsToPush.length, rowsToPush[0].length)
                         .setValues(rowsToPush);
            }
          });

          // Delete temp file
          Drive.Files.remove(tempFile.id);
        }
      });
    });
    thread.removeLabel(label);
  });
}

function isHeaderRowDates(row) {
  // Simple check: do we see a date object in the first few cells?
  for (let i=0; i<row.length; i++) {
    if (Object.prototype.toString.call(row[i]) === '[object Date]') return true;
  }
  return false;
}

Part 4: Connecting to Lovable

Now that your data is in the Sheet and you have your Service Account Key:

  1. In your Lovable project (or the code it generated), you are likely using a library to fetch data.
  2. If Lovable allows you to add Environment Variables (or Secrets), you will add your Service Account JSON there.
  3. If Lovable is generating a React/Node app, you will use the google-spreadsheet npm package.

Does your Lovable project have a "Database" or "Integrations" tab, or did it just export code for you to host? This determines exactly where you paste that Service Account Key.
